bull_bear.body: The company's credit rating is closely tied to its ability to manage its debt and maintain a stable financial position, and any changes in the credit rating outlook could have a significant impact on the company's financial health.
bull_bear.title: Non-obvious takeaways

bull_bear.body:
- Describes itself as India's first largest bitumen company in the private sector, with market share gained over the years on product quality and customer satisfaction and no identified identical business peer
- Forward integration: bitumen manufacturing is an extension of the parent bitumen bulk transportation business
- Amongst the largest operators of specialised bitumen and LPG tanker fleets in India, supporting supply reliability and customer comfort
- Bulk bitumen storage terminals near ports enable an import-led sourcing strategy and optimum handling of imports, reducing dependency on oil companies
- Geographically spread manufacturing, storage and terminal network across North, West, South, East and North-East India
- Long-standing supplier and client relationships, including tanker contracts with HPCL, BPCL and IOCL
- Promoters with 38-plus years of industry experience
- Consistent dividend-paying record
- Major capex to date funded from capital infusion and internal accruals, saving financial costs
- In-house authorised Ashok Leyland service centre plus own workshops, giving faster fleet turnaround at lower cost
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Import dependence on timely, correctly priced and correct-quality shipments — The Company runs an import-led sourcing strategy for bitumen and names imports - shipments at the right time, right pricing and quality material - as one of its explicit challenges. Sourcing disruption or adverse import pricing hits both cost of goods and the ability to supply a network of port-linked terminals.
- Crude-linked input cost volatility amplified by geopolitics — Management states that global geopolitical uncertainty, supply-chain disruption and war in the Middle East produced heightened input cost pressures and supply-side constraints, affecting market pricing, margins and profitability. Bitumen is a refinery residue of heavy crude, so the input cost is outside the Company's control.
- Price competition in a commoditised product with large state-owned rivals — The Company lists pricing - competition with other players in the industry - as a challenge, and names IOCL, HPCL, BPCL and ONGC among the major players in the India bitumen market. Competing on a commoditised binder against refiners who also supply its logistics contracts limits pricing power; management separately notes intensified competition across the industry during the year.
- Dependence on government infrastructure spending and counterparty payment cycles — Demand is tied to road construction under government priority programmes, and the Company explicitly flags timely payment to our clients from the related government authorities as a challenge, alongside continuous development of the infrastructure sector. A slowdown in road capex or stretched contractor/authority payments flows straight into volumes and working capital.
- Demand concentration in a single end-use and a narrow customer set — The Company's own market commentary puts roughly 88% to 96% of domestic bitumen consumption into road construction, and most of its bitumen and LPG tankers are under contract with HPCL, BPCL and IOCL. That leaves little diversification if road demand or those oil-company contracts weaken.
- Seasonality of revenue across all three businesses — The Company states its bitumen, logistics and wind-power businesses are seasonal in nature, due to which revenue gets varied; its own industry commentary cites monsoon pacing as a driver of Indian supply-chain dynamics. Seasonality makes quarterly results and fixed-cost absorption uneven.
- Macroeconomic, policy, tax, interest-rate and exchange-rate exposure acknowledged as outside management's control — The forward-looking-statement caution and the Threats section both name changes in government policies and regulations, tax regimes, economic developments in India and the countries where the Company operates, and fluctuations in exchange and interest rates. Exchange-rate exposure is structural given import-led sourcing and a UAE subsidiary.
- Safety and hazardous-cargo handling risk in LPG and heated bitumen logistics — The Company notes LPG is highly inflammable and requires tankers that address all safety aspects during loading, transport and unloading, while bulk bitumen moves in heated, insulated tankers. An incident in own-fleet hazardous transport carries operational, legal and reputational consequences.
- Credit rating on a negative outlook — CRISIL has assigned/affirmed a long-term rating of CRISIL A with a Negative outlook on the Company's working capital limits including the Working Capital Demand Loan. For an import-led, working-capital-intensive trading and manufacturing model, a negative outlook signals possible pressure on the cost and availability of that funding.
- Management's own framing understates threat exposure — The Threats section asserts there are no major business or industry threats before us, while the same report documents a 32.93% revenue decline, a 39.08% fall in bitumen volumes, margin pressure from input costs and competition, and a negative rating outlook. Readers should weigh the disclosed operating facts over the self-assessment.

business.title: Segment / subsidiary detail

business.body: AICL manufactures and trades bitumen and allied bituminous products used heavily in infrastructure and road-construction projects, and provides logistics for bulk bitumen and LPG through its own fleet of specialised insulated tankers. Most of its bitumen and LPG tankers are contracted to major Indian oil companies such as HPCL, BPCL and IOCL, alongside other large industrial consumers of the product. The Company also generates power through wind mills in Rajasthan and Maharashtra, and runs an in-house authorised Ashok Leyland service centre to maintain its own tanker fleet; management notes these businesses are seasonal, so revenue varies.

outlook.body: The company's growth prospects are tied to its ability to manage its debt and maintain a stable financial position, as well as its ability to expand its operations and increase its revenue.
outlook.title: Growth verticals / optionality

outlook.body:
- Scale an import-led bitumen sourcing strategy, maintaining a high-capacity network of port-linked, company-owned bulk storage terminals plus outsourced storage at Karwar and Haldia to handle, store and distribute imported bitumen nationwide
- Use the Karwar acquisition (Konkan Storage Systems (Karwar) Private Limited, effective 29 January 2026) to reinforce import-sourcing capability and the coastal infrastructure footprint through port-based bulk liquid storage and terminal facilities
- Stay diversified across three legs — bitumen manufacturing and trading, bulk bitumen and LPG tanker logistics, and wind power — with bitumen manufacturing framed as forward integration from the parent bitumen bulk transportation business
- Prioritise cost management, operational efficiency and resource optimisation to protect margins in a volatile input-cost environment
- Pursue growth through strategically aligned wholly-owned subsidiaries in India and overseas, with AICL Overseas FZ-LLC (Ras Al Khaimah, UAE) focused on global ship chartering and maritime logistics under RBI ODI guidelines
- Deepen regional reach via outsourced storage positioned to capitalise on localised infrastructure, and through the Cochin subsidiary serving Southern India infrastructure demand
- Keep tanker fleet availability high using an in-house authorised Ashok Leyland service centre and own workshops at Mumbai, Baroda and Jodhpur for faster, cheaper fleet turnaround
- Explore new market opportunities while strengthening business fundamentals (management's stated intent, not a quantified plan)
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: The annual report describes footprint rather than named expansion projects with timelines. The Company's stated infrastructure comprises manufacturing and storage units at Taloja (Maharashtra), Belgaum (Karnataka), Baroda (Gujarat), Hyderabad (Telangana), Rangia (Dist. Kamrup, Assam) and Pachpadra City (Dist. Barmer, Rajasthan), with Cochin (Kerala) operated through the wholly-owned subsidiary Bituminex Cochin Private Limited; liquid bulk storage and terminal facilities at Mangalore, Baroda, Dighi and Taloja; company-owned and maintained import terminals at Dighi, Mumbai, Vadodara, Hazira (loading facility), Mangalore and West Bengal; and strategic outsourced storage at Karwar (Karnataka) and Haldia (West Bengal) to expand regional distribution reach. The one completed inorganic addition in the year is Konkan Storage Systems (Karwar) Private Limited, acquired fully effective January 29, 2026, which manages port-based bulk liquid storage and terminal facilities at Karwar and which the Company says significantly reinforces its import-sourcing capability and coastal infrastructure footprint. Wind power comprises one windmill at Dhulia (Maharashtra) and one at Jaisalmer (Rajasthan). On the sustainability side, the BRSR records that environmentally/socially targeted capex was 1.99% of turnover in FY2025 for installation of solar plants at Taloja, Dighi and Baroda, and 0% in FY2026. Expansion language beyond this is opportunity framing rather than committed projects: the Company cites a huge deficit in indigenous bitumen supply leaving scope for imports, a power demand-supply deficit leaving scope for expansion of wind power mills, and tremendous scope for developing value-added products - none of these carries a capacity number, a project name or a commissioning date. AICL Finance Private Limited has not yet commenced business activities and awaits statutory approvals. No installed capacity figures and no BRSR Section A plant/capacity table appear in this bundle.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Management frames baseline bitumen demand as dictated by government infrastructure programmes — Bharatmala Pariyojana, PM Gati Shakti and continuing national highway expansion beyond 146,000 km
- Approximately 88% to 96% of domestic bitumen consumption is stated to flow directly into road construction, so the business is tied to road capex
- India is described as one of the fastest-expanding bitumen markets, with consumption around 8.5 to 8.8 million metric tonnes and a CAGR of roughly 4%; the market is valued between about $3.45 billion and $4.57 billion
- Indian supply chain characterised as heavily reliant on domestic refinery yields augmented by structural imports, and as heavily influenced by contractor liquidity and monsoon pacing
- A stated huge deficit between indigenous bitumen supply and demand is presented as the opportunity underpinning the import-led model, with own plants and bulk imports minimising dependency on oil companies
- Product mix trend: viscosity-graded bitumen, particularly VG30, anchors the Indian market at close to half the product share, while polymer-modified binders are seeing fast adoption on high-speed expressways
- Value-added products are cited as offering tremendous scope for higher margins
- Regional demand concentration: North India holds the largest share at about 38%, with West and South India following, linked to refiners IOCL, BPCL, HPCL and MRPL
- Headwinds management flags: global geopolitical uncertainty, supply-chain disruption and war in the Middle East producing heightened input-cost pressure, supply-side constraints and intensified competition that affected market pricing, margins and profitability
- Seasonality: the bitumen, logistics and power businesses are described as seasonal in nature, so revenue varies through the year
- Stated opportunity in wind power from a described deficit between power demand and supply, leaving scope to expand wind mills
- Environmental transition in the Indian market toward warm-mix asphalt, rubber-modified roads and localised emission targets
outlook.title: Demand & outlook drivers

deepdive.thesis: Agarwal Industrial Corporation Limited has received a credit rating of Crisil A/Negative from CRISIL, indicating a stable outlook with some negative factors, and has a total bank loan facility of Rs. 240 crore. The company's financial health is being closely monitored by CRISIL, and the rating is subject to revision based on new information or unavailability of information. The company's ability to manage its debt and maintain a stable financial position will be crucial in determining its future credit rating.

The Group says it will continue prudent cost management, operational efficiency and resource optimisation while pursuing sustainable growth and improved profitability in the periods ahead.
AICL Finance Private Limited has not yet commenced business activities and is in the process of obtaining the necessary statutory approvals.

Management explicitly flags geopolitical uncertainty, supply-chain disruption and the war in the Middle East as driving input-cost pressure, supply-side constraints and intensified competition that affect pricing, margins and profitability.
Among its stated challenges the Company flags timely payment from the related government authorities, alongside import shipment timing/pricing/quality and industry price competition.
Management cites a huge deficit between power demand and supply as leaving tremendous scope for expansion of its wind power mills - stated as an opportunity, with no capacity, cost or date committed.
Management identifies tremendous scope for developing value-added bitumen products with potential for higher margins, framed as an opportunity rather than a sanctioned project.

risks.risk: Import dependence on timely, correctly priced and correct-quality shipments
risks.note: The Company runs an import-led sourcing strategy for bitumen and names imports - shipments at the right time, right pricing and quality material - as one of its explicit challenges. Sourcing disruption or adverse import pricing hits both cost of goods and the ability to supply a network of port-linked terminals.

risks.risk: Crude-linked input cost volatility amplified by geopolitics
risks.note: Management states that global geopolitical uncertainty, supply-chain disruption and war in the Middle East produced heightened input cost pressures and supply-side constraints, affecting market pricing, margins and profitability. Bitumen is a refinery residue of heavy crude, so the input cost is outside the Company's control.

risks.risk: Price competition in a commoditised product with large state-owned rivals
risks.note: The Company lists pricing - competition with other players in the industry - as a challenge, and names IOCL, HPCL, BPCL and ONGC among the major players in the India bitumen market. Competing on a commoditised binder against refiners who also supply its logistics contracts limits pricing power; management separately notes intensified competition across the industry during the year.

risks.risk: Dependence on government infrastructure spending and counterparty payment cycles
risks.note: Demand is tied to road construction under government priority programmes, and the Company explicitly flags timely payment to our clients from the related government authorities as a challenge, alongside continuous development of the infrastructure sector. A slowdown in road capex or stretched contractor/authority payments flows straight into volumes and working capital.

risks.risk: Demand concentration in a single end-use and a narrow customer set
risks.note: The Company's own market commentary puts roughly 88% to 96% of domestic bitumen consumption into road construction, and most of its bitumen and LPG tankers are under contract with HPCL, BPCL and IOCL. That leaves little diversification if road demand or those oil-company contracts weaken.

risks.risk: Seasonality of revenue across all three businesses
risks.note: The Company states its bitumen, logistics and wind-power businesses are seasonal in nature, due to which revenue gets varied; its own industry commentary cites monsoon pacing as a driver of Indian supply-chain dynamics. Seasonality makes quarterly results and fixed-cost absorption uneven.

risks.risk: Macroeconomic, policy, tax, interest-rate and exchange-rate exposure acknowledged as outside management's control
risks.note: The forward-looking-statement caution and the Threats section both name changes in government policies and regulations, tax regimes, economic developments in India and the countries where the Company operates, and fluctuations in exchange and interest rates. Exchange-rate exposure is structural given import-led sourcing and a UAE subsidiary.

risks.risk: Safety and hazardous-cargo handling risk in LPG and heated bitumen logistics
risks.note: The Company notes LPG is highly inflammable and requires tankers that address all safety aspects during loading, transport and unloading, while bulk bitumen moves in heated, insulated tankers. An incident in own-fleet hazardous transport carries operational, legal and reputational consequences.

risks.risk: Credit rating on a negative outlook
risks.note: CRISIL has assigned/affirmed a long-term rating of CRISIL A with a Negative outlook on the Company's working capital limits including the Working Capital Demand Loan. For an import-led, working-capital-intensive trading and manufacturing model, a negative outlook signals possible pressure on the cost and availability of that funding.

risks.risk: Management's own framing understates threat exposure
risks.note: The Threats section asserts there are no major business or industry threats before us, while the same report documents a 32.93% revenue decline, a 39.08% fall in bitumen volumes, margin pressure from input costs and competition, and a negative rating outlook. Readers should weigh the disclosed operating facts over the self-assessment.

one_liner.title: One Liner (RHP)
one_liner.body: Agarwal Industrial Corporation Limited (AICL) is an Ancillary Infra player describing itself as India's first largest bitumen company in the private sector, combining bitumen manufacturing and trading with specialised bulk bitumen and LPG tanker logistics and a small wind-power portfolio.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: AICL manufactures and trades bitumen and allied bituminous products used heavily in infrastructure and road-construction projects, and provides logistics for bulk bitumen and LPG through its own fleet of specialised insulated tankers. Most of its bitumen and LPG tankers are contracted to major Indian oil companies such as HPCL, BPCL and IOCL, alongside other large industrial consumers of the product. The Company also generates power through wind mills in Rajasthan and Maharashtra, and runs an in-house authorised Ashok Leyland service centre to maintain its own tanker fleet; management notes these businesses are seasonal, so revenue varies.

- AICL Overseas FZ-LLC — subsidiary: Wholly owned overseas subsidiary, 100% held, based in Ras Al Khaimah, UAE; focuses on global ship chartering and maritime logistics under RBI Overseas Direct Investment guidelines; designated a material subsidiary under Regulation 16(1)(c) of the Listing Regulations, with Independent Woman Director Ms. Khushboo Lalji on its board; related-party counterparty for interest, guarantee commission and inter-company loans
- Agarwal Translink Private Limited — subsidiary: Wholly owned Indian subsidiary, 100% held; primary logistics arm managing overland transportation of bitumen, LPG and Low Sulphur Heavy Stock (LSHS), owning a specialised bitumen tanker fleet and operating a BPCL retail petroleum outlet at Shahpur, Asangaon (Maharashtra); related-party counterparty for freight, transportation and labour charges and purchase/sale of HSD, oil and spare parts
- AICL Finance Private Limited — subsidiary: Wholly owned Indian subsidiary, 100% held; yet to commence business activities and in the process of obtaining the necessary statutory approvals; listed in AOC-1 notes as a subsidiary yet to commence operations

products.body:

end_markets.body:

- Major domestic oil companies (HPCL, BPCL, IOCL) as tanker logistics customers

growth_optionality.body: The company's growth prospects are tied to its ability to manage its debt and maintain a stable financial position, as well as its ability to expand its operations and increase its revenue.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Management frames baseline bitumen demand as dictated by government infrastructure programmes — Bharatmala Pariyojana, PM Gati Shakti and continuing national highway expansion beyond 146,000 km
- Approximately 88% to 96% of domestic bitumen consumption is stated to flow directly into road construction, so the business is tied to road capex
- India is described as one of the fastest-expanding bitumen markets, with consumption around 8.5 to 8.8 million metric tonnes and a CAGR of roughly 4%; the market is valued between about $3.45 billion and $4.57 billion
- Indian supply chain characterised as heavily reliant on domestic refinery yields augmented by structural imports, and as heavily influenced by contractor liquidity and monsoon pacing
- A stated huge deficit between indigenous bitumen supply and demand is presented as the opportunity underpinning the import-led model, with own plants and bulk imports minimising dependency on oil companies
- Product mix trend: viscosity-graded bitumen, particularly VG30, anchors the Indian market at close to half the product share, while polymer-modified binders are seeing fast adoption on high-speed expressways
- Value-added products are cited as offering tremendous scope for higher margins
- Regional demand concentration: North India holds the largest share at about 38%, with West and South India following, linked to refiners IOCL, BPCL, HPCL and MRPL
- Headwinds management flags: global geopolitical uncertainty, supply-chain disruption and war in the Middle East producing heightened input-cost pressure, supply-side constraints and intensified competition that affected market pricing, margins and profitability
- Seasonality: the bitumen, logistics and power businesses are described as seasonal in nature, so revenue varies through the year
- Stated opportunity in wind power from a described deficit between power demand and supply, leaving scope to expand wind mills
- Environmental transition in the Indian market toward warm-mix asphalt, rubber-modified roads and localised emission targets

The one completed inorganic addition in the year is Konkan Storage Systems (Karwar) Private Limited, acquired fully effective January 29, 2026, which manages port-based bulk liquid storage and terminal facilities at Karwar and which the Company says significantly reinforces its import-sourcing capability and coastal infrastructure footprint.
